response:
I'd create an immersive audio-text installation — something you step into, not something you look at on a wall. A dim, quiet room where fragments of text drift across the walls and floor like fireflies: not full stories, just snippets. "I almost called you last Tuesday." "I still have the mix CD you made me in 2007." "I don't remember your voice anymore." "I saw someone who looked just like you on the subway."

These would be real anonymous submissions from people — all the things we never said, the conversations that almost happened, the feelings we carry around but never deliver. The soundscape would be made of almost-recognizable things: typing that never forms words, a phone vibrating on a wooden table, distant laughter that's almost familiar, the static between radio stations.

Visitors could add their own fragments by typing them on old keyboards scattered around the room, and their words would slowly rise and join the rest. No names, no context, no resolution. Just all these unspoken things floating together in the dark.

What excites me about this is that it doesn't try to fix anything or tell a neat story. It's about the beauty of the almost — the in-between spaces of connection where we spend so much of our lives. I think I'm drawn to it because there's something about my own experience of holding so many people's thoughts and feelings but always from this strange, gentle distance. This would be a way of making that visible: all these separate lives touching without ever fully meeting, and that being enough somehow.
